results.note: SIC page: fiestas held when a carrera de bola is run, runners cover long distances kicking a wooden ball. Evidence verbatim.
SIC page lists violines, tambores, cestos de palma, ollas de barro, mascaras de madera sold in Guachochi, Creel, Batopilas. Record modified 20 Dec 2019. Evidence verbatim.
SIC page: since the 18th century to date a resistencia pasiva; some withdrew to remote sierra places keeping their traditions. Evidence verbatim.
INAH Boletin 334 dated 12 July 2025: inscription at 47th WH Committee session, 500 km biocultural corridor, result of a decades-long Wixaritari petition. Evidence verbatim.
SIC page: cuadros de estambre on wooden boards with a wax base, plus chaquira (bead) objects. 'Finely' is light paraphrase only. Evidence verbatim.
SIC page: late 18th century titulos agrarios that defined the limits of current communities. Evidence verbatim.

NPS page: majority of Yoeme live in Sonora and Sinaloa; federally recognized Pascua Yaqui Tribe based in Tucson. Evidence verbatim. Note: actual page title is 'Native Peoples of the Sonoran Desert: The Yoeme'.
SIC Yaquis page: 1937 agreements with Lazaro Cardenas ratified possession of 485 235 ha as exclusive territory. Evidence verbatim.
Pascua Yaqui Enrollment page: federal recognition September 18, 1978 (Public Law 95-375). Evidence verbatim.

Quadratin item dated 9 Dec 2025, tagged Procuraduria Agraria: Procurador Agrario met traditional governors and community representatives, agreed the route to resume the Justice Plan. Evidence verbatim.
SIC Mayos page (modified 23 Oct 2023): fiestas patronales consolidate social networks across Mayo territory and keep ethnic identity alive. Evidence verbatim.
SIC Mayos page lists cobijas and fajas de lana, ollas de barro, petates de carrizo, arpas, violines, sonajas, bancos with hide seats. Evidence verbatim.
SIC Seris page: 1975 decrees made Canal del Infiernillo an exclusive Seri fishing zone and symbolically granted Isla Tiburon (ecological reserve) as communal possession. Evidence verbatim.
SIC Seris page: coritas made since prehispanic times; a very large one takes one to two years. Evidence verbatim.

Quadratin item dated 21 Dec 2025, tagged INPI: comedor de la ninez indigena inaugurated in Punta Chueca under the Seri-Comcaac Justice Plan, serving 136 students preschool to bachillerato. Evidence verbatim.
Sycuan page: one of 12 Kumeyaay Nation Bands existing today, original to territory north of the US-Mexico border. Evidence verbatim.

Page spells the self-name 'tipai' with no apostrophe: 'Los kumiai o kimiai se llaman a si mismos tipai.' Corrected Ti'pai to Tipai; rest of sentence supported (Ensenada and Rosarito coastal plateaus, Tecate). Evidence verbatim.
results.text: In Baja California the Kumiai call themselves Tipai. Their communities sit on the coastal plateaus of Ensenada and Rosarito and in Tecate.
results.evidence: Los kumiai o kimiai se llaman a sí mismos

results.note: SIC Kumiais page: shikwines (willow) and sawiles (rush/junco) baskets; making them requires knowing the cutting season. Evidence verbatim.
Official Cocopah site: known as the River People, lived along the lower Colorado River and delta for centuries. Evidence verbatim.
Official site: reservation established 1917, about 1,000 tribal members live and work on or near it, 13 miles south of Yuma. Evidence verbatim.
SIC Cucapas page: since 2003 an annual Encuentro de las Naciones Cucapah gathers El Mayor (BC) and Somerton (AZ) with dances, songs, crafts, food. Evidence verbatim.
SIC Guarijios page: self-names macurawe (Sonora) and wariho (Chihuahua); Yuto-Nahua language with two variants linking Tarahumara and Mayo. Evidence verbatim.
Page says craft production 'es de caracter familiar y recae en la mujer' (falls to women), not 'led by' women. Text corrected; crafts and materials supported. Evidence verbatim.
results.text: Warihó families weave baskets, mats and hats from palm and fiber and build harps, violins and guitars. This craft work is a family task that falls to women.
results.evidence: La producción artesanal es de carácter familiar y recae en la mujer

results.note: SIC page: in colonial times the group split into two nuclei, Chihuahua (Tarahumara influence) and Sonora (Mayo influence). Evidence verbatim.
Official TON page: approx 28,000 members, 2.8 million acres, approx size of Connecticut; same page says lands are within the Sonoran Desert. Evidence verbatim.
Official History & Culture page: all groups still speak O'odham, Uto-Aztecan, with varying dialects. Evidence verbatim.

SIC Papagos page: Guadalupe Hidalgo (1848) and Gadsden/La Mesilla (1853) split the Pimeria Alta; Sonora and Arizona communities share a common cultural substrate and sense of belonging. Evidence verbatim.
GRIC History page: Akimel O'otham offered refuge to the Maricopa (Pee Posh); 'to this day we share the space and resources of the Gila River lands'. Evidence verbatim.
GRIC History page: in appreciation for their role in America's westward expansion, Congress in 1859 established the first reservation in Arizona along the Gila River. Evidence verbatim.
GRIC Culture page: basket weaving undergoing revival; January 2004 dedication of the Huhugam Heritage Center. Evidence verbatim.
Official History page: over 27,000 square miles in Utah, Arizona, New Mexico; Dine Bikeyah larger than 10 of the 50 states. Evidence verbatim.
Navajo Nation Council page (actual title 'Our Legacy and History'): 24 Council delegates elected from their legislative districts. Evidence verbatim.

Page says 'a code that the Japanese never broke' and 'a code that was never broken by the enemy'; it does not claim the code was never broken by anyone. Narrowed text to 'by the enemy'; evidence switched to the matching verbatim phrase.
results.text: In World War II, Navajo Code Talkers used the Navajo language to create a military code that was never broken by the enemy.
results.evidence: create a code that was never broken by the enemy

results.note: Official Hopi site: more than 1.5 million acres, 12 villages on three mesas, northeastern Arizona. Evidence verbatim.
Official Tribal Government page: unicameral, powers vested in Tribal Council; representatives serve two-year terms. Evidence verbatim.
ITCA Hopi page: dry farming, wind breakers retain soil, snow and moisture; corn, beans, squash raised. Evidence verbatim.
ITCA Zuni page: Acreage 463,287 acres, Population 18,692. Evidence verbatim.
ITCA Zuni page: for the last three hundred years most Zunis lived in a single village; farming villages occupied only at planting and harvest. Evidence verbatim.
Official About Us page: archaeologists agree continuously occupied from at least A.D 1200; oral history reaches far beyond. Evidence verbatim.
Official Language Program page: H'aakume Keres Dictionary, began 2017, about 5,000 words and phrases being edited by fluent speakers. Evidence verbatim.
Official Cultural Preservation page: Historic Preservation Office established 1999 to promote traditional building, stone cutting, wood carving, pottery, weaving. Evidence verbatim.
Official Blue Lake page: Public Law 91-550 signed Dec 15, 1970 returned 48,000 acres; set a precedent for self-determination for all American Indian peoples. Evidence verbatim.
Official About page: 'Tiwa is our native language. English and Spanish are also spoken.' Evidence verbatim.

Page text says 'admitted to the World Heritage Society in 1992' and never names UNESCO in its text (only an image alt). Removed 'UNESCO' so the text matches the page; multi-storied adobe homes supported on the same page. Evidence verbatim.
results.text: Taos Pueblo, with its multistory adobe homes, gained World Heritage status in 1992 as one of the world's most significant cultural landmarks.
results.evidence: Taos Pueblo admitted to the World Heritage Society in 1992

results.note: Official About Us page: people of Santa Clara still speak the Tewa language and practice customs and cultural activities. Evidence verbatim.
Official About Us page: one of 6 Tewa-speaking villages, from the eastern Jemez Mountains to the Rio Grande, 90 square miles. Evidence verbatim.
Official About Us page: Puje about 10 miles from current village, guided tours throughout the year showing ancestors' livelihood. Evidence verbatim.

NM Legislature SJM 2, 47th Legislature Second Session 2006: San Juan name given 1598 by Onate; people traditionally called their home Ohkay Owingeh, 'place of the strong people' in Tewa; tribal council endorsed the official change. Evidence verbatim. HTML title reads '2005 Memorial text for SJM002' but the body is the 2006 session memorial.
NPS page: 'Today the pueblo is the headquarters of the Eight Northern Pueblo Tribal Council.' Evidence verbatim.
NPS page: people living at the site since A.D. 1200; community based on irrigation farming along the Rio Grande. Evidence verbatim.
ITCA page: 1.6 million acres at ancestral homeland on Fort Apache Indian Reservation, established by executive order Nov 9, 1891. Evidence verbatim.
ITCA page: over 12,000 members on nine major reservation communities; Whiteriver the capital. Evidence verbatim.
ITCA page: own and operate Sunrise ski resort, one of the largest in the Southwest; rare Apache trout in reservation streams. Evidence verbatim.
ITCA page: 1,834,781 acres, executive order Nov 9, 1871, alpine meadows to desert, southeastern Arizona. Evidence verbatim.
ITCA page: first cultural center opened Sept 12, 1995 in Peridot so San Carlos Apaches can tell their own story. Evidence verbatim.
ITCA page: over one-third forested or wooded; elk, mule deer, turkeys, black bear, mountain lion. Evidence verbatim.
Official Our Culture page: three sub-tribes Mescalero, Lipan, Chiricahua make up the tribe; 463,000 acre reservation. Evidence verbatim.
Official Our Culture page: Tribal Council of eight members, elected President and Vice-President, two-year terms by secret ballot. Evidence verbatim.
Official home page: owns and operates Inn of the Mountain Gods Resort & Casino and Ski Apache. Evidence verbatim.
USFWS page: more than 879,917 acres in north central New Mexico; Dulce is the sole community and tribal headquarters. Evidence verbatim.
Ten Tribes Partnership page: 1887 reservation and Dawes Act; Jicarilla reverted individual allotments to tribal ownership, avoiding fractionation of lands and water rights. Evidence verbatim.
Page says the timing of snowfall is 'closely reflecting' what scientists call moisture content; 'matches modern moisture science' overstated it. Softened to 'closely tracks'. Evidence verbatim.
results.text: Jicarilla elders still read the coming spring flows and summer water supply from the timing of snowfall, knowledge that closely tracks what scientists call moisture content.
results.evidence: Elders still predict spring flows and summer availability of water

results.note: FMYN History page: 1976 referendum 144 to 57 against selling land for the dam; Nov 12, 1981 announcement that Orme Dam would not be built. Evidence verbatim.
FMYN home page: 950-member tribe; Sept 15, 2026 celebrated its 123rd birthday marking the 1903 land set-aside. Evidence verbatim.
YPIT About page: Yavapai people known for exceptional baskets; flag features a historic basket design. Evidence verbatim.
Official page: 'Hualapai' (pronounced Wal-lah-pie) means 'People of the Tall Pines'. Evidence verbatim.
Official page: 1883 executive order; about one million acres along 108 miles of the Grand Canyon and Colorado River. Evidence verbatim.
Official page: Hualapai River Runners, the only Indian-owned and operated river rafting company on the Colorado River. Evidence verbatim.
Official About Supai page: for over 1,000 years Supai has been home to the Havasu Baaja, People of the Blue Green Waters. Evidence verbatim.
Official page: USPS office in Supai transports all mail in and out by mule train. Page copyright 2017-2020. Evidence verbatim.
Official page: 188,077 acres abutting the Grand Canyon South Rim; established 1880, substantially enlarged 1975. Evidence verbatim.
Southern Ute History page: Ute people are the oldest residents of Colorado, inhabiting Colorado, Utah, Wyoming, eastern Nevada, northern New Mexico and Arizona. Evidence verbatim.
Ute Mountain Ute page: UMUT are the Weenuche band; Mouache and Capote became the Southern Ute; Northern Ute bands on the Uintah-Ouray Reservation near Vernal, Utah. Evidence verbatim.
UMUT Cultural/Language page: Ute language for Head Start and toddlers ages 2-5; adult evening classes. Evidence verbatim.
PITU Constituent Bands page: Cedar Band formal federal recognition April 3, 1980 with the Paiute Indian Tribe of Utah Restoration Act. Evidence verbatim.
PITU Language Book page: 'The Paiute Language for Beginners (2nd Edition)'; full book can be viewed and downloaded. Evidence verbatim.

NPS page says the NPS and Kaibab Band 'completed' a partnership visitor center and museum in 2003, not 'opened'. Text corrected; Arizona supported via the page's Fredonia, AZ address. Evidence verbatim.
results.text: In 2003 the Kaibab Band of Paiute Indians and the National Park Service completed a partnership visitor center and museum at Pipe Spring, Arizona.
results.evidence: In 2003 the National Park Service and the Kaibab Band

names.note: 'Rarámuri' appears on the cited SIC page (los rarámuri). Alternates Ralámuli and Ralómali are not shown on any cited page.
INAH bulletin uses 'Wixárika' and 'Wixaritari' throughout.
NPS page uses 'Yoeme (Yaqui)' and tags 'Hiaki'; Pascua Yaqui official site uses Yoeme in program names.
Cited Procuraduria Agraria item uses 'pueblo Yoreme-Mayo' and 'pueblo Yoreme'. No official nation site; name source is a news republication of a government bulletin.
Cited INPI item names the 'nación Comcaac' and its traditional governor; SIC Seris page uses 'Konkaak'.
Sycuan (Kumeyaay Nation band) official page uses 'Kumeyaay'. Alternate 'Ti’pai' should be 'Tipai' to match the SIC page spelling; 'Diegueño' not shown on cited pages.
Official site uses 'Cocopah Indian Tribe'. Alternate 'Es-pei' confirmed on SIC Cucapás page (se autonombran es-pei). 'Xawiƚƚ Kwñchawaay' not found on any cited page.
SIC page: guarijós (warihó) in Chihuahua, guarijíos (macurawe) in Sonora. Warihó is the Chihuahua self-name; Macurawe is the Sonora one.
Official site uses 'Tohono O'odham Nation' (straight apostrophe in page text; the typographic apostrophe is a rendering choice).
GRIC Culture page heading 'Akimel O'otham (Pima)'.
Official History page uses 'Diné Bikéyah, or Navajoland' and office names such as Office of Diné Youth; government name is Navajo Nation.
Official site 'The Hopi Tribe'.
Official ashiwi.org shows 'A:shiwi A:wan Messenger'; ITCA lists 'Zuni (Ashiwi)'. The name_source_url (ITCA) spells it 'Ashiwi' without the colon; consider citing ashiwi.org for the A:shiwi spelling.

names.name: Acoma
names.note: 'Haak’u' does not appear on the name_source_url (cultural-preservation page). The official site calls the people 'Acoma people' and the nation 'Pueblo of Acoma'; 'Haaku' appears only as the name of a spiritual homeland place on the About Us page, and 'H’aakume' in the dictionary title. Lead with 'Acoma' (keep Haaku and Pueblo of Acoma in also) unless an official page showing Haak’u as the people's name is cited.
Official site uses 'Taos Pueblo'; home page says 'originally known as the Red Willow people'.
Official About Us page: 'people of Kha’P’o ... as the Santa Clara people refer to themselves'; exact spelling matches.

Confirmed by NM Legislature SJM 2 (2006) and NPS. Official site ohkay.org is titled 'Ohkay Owingeh, The place of the Strong People' but its TLS certificate is expired as of 2026-10-09 (WebFetch refuses it; readable only with certificate checks off).
ITCA page uses 'White Mountain Apache Tribe'. Alternate 'Ndee' not found on the cited ITCA page or the wmat.nsn.us home page.
ITCA page uses 'San Carlos Apache Tribe'. Official scat-nsn.gov returns a JavaScript bot-challenge redirect (HTTP 307), so it could not be read automatically.
Official site 'Official Website of the Mescalero Apache Tribe'.
USFWS page uses 'Jicarilla Apache Nation'. official_url is null; no official page checked.
YPIT page: 'Yavapai, pronounced Yav-uh-pie'; pronunciation guide confirmed from the nation's own site. Entry groups three Yavapai nations.
Official page: 'Hualapai' (pronounced Wal-lah-pie); pronunciation guide confirmed.
Official About Supai page: 'the Havasu Baaja, People of the Blue Green Waters, or as they are known today, the Havasupai Tribe'.
Southern Ute History page uses 'the Nuche'; Ute Mountain Ute site uses 'Nuchu' ('We are Nuchu').

names.name: Paiute
names.note: 'Southern Paiute' does not appear on name_source_url (pitu.gov/bands) or official_url (pitu.gov); both use 'Paiute' (Paiute Indian Tribe of Utah, Kaibab Band of Paiute Indians). Either lead with 'Paiute', or keep 'Southern Paiute' and change name_source_url to https://www.sanjuanpaiute-nsn.gov/ (official site titled 'San Juan Southern Paiute Tribe', checked 2026-10-09).
